Bostock v. Clayton County. In June 2020, the Supreme Court ruled six to three that the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits employment discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote the majority opinion, which consolidated three separate cases of workers fired or terminated for their sexual orientation or gender identity. Gorsuch held that discrimination based on these characteristics necessarily involves discrimination because of sex, and therefore violates Title VII regardless of the employer's stated motivation. His reasoning was textualist, focusing on the statute's language. The statute's prohibition on discrimination because of sex covers causation, and discrimination against same-sex or transgender employees inherently involves sex as a causal factor. The ruling immediately extended federal employment protections to millions of LGBTQ workers across all jurisdictions. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito dissented, arguing that the decision rewrote a statute Congress had never intended to cover sexual orientation or gender identity. While the decision represented a major civil rights victory for workplace equality, it expressly did not address religious exemptions, leaving open questions about how sexual orientation and gender identity protections interact with religious freedom claims in employment contexts.
